lesson.title: What the Meter Actually Reads: Average Power
lesson.summary: Average power strips away the oscillating part of instantaneous power to reveal the steady rate at which an AC circuit actually consumes energy, and rms values make that formula simple.
lesson.body:
Instantaneous power swings wildly over each cycle, rising and falling twice per period and sometimes dipping negative, so it is not what a wattmeter reports or what an electric bill charges for. What matters practically is average power, P, the average of p(t) over one full cycle, because that average is the steady rate at which energy is actually consumed by the load, regardless of how it wiggles instant to instant.

From the instantaneous power expansion, p(t) = (VmIm/2)[cos θ + cos(2ωt − θ)], averaging over a full period eliminates the oscillating cos(2ωt − θ) term entirely, since a cosine averages to exactly zero over any whole number of its own cycles. What remains is P = (VmIm/2) cos θ. Rewriting peak amplitudes as rms values, Vrms = Vm/√2 and Irms = Im/√2, so VmIm/2 = Vrms Irms, gives the standard working formula: P = Vrms Irms cos θ. This is precisely why rms values exist: they are defined so this simple, DC-like power formula holds for AC circuits without extra factors of 2 or √2 cluttering every calculation.

For the series RL circuit, Vrms = 120 V, Irms = 2.4 A, and θ = 53.13°, current lagging voltage, the impedance angle of Z = 50∠53.13° Ω found earlier. Average power is P = 120 × 2.4 × cos(53.13°) = 288 × 0.6000 = 172.8 W. This matches, within normal rounding, the constant term, 172.9 W, computed directly from the instantaneous power expression in the previous section; the small difference comes only from rounding Im to 3.39 A rather than carrying full precision.

The cos θ factor is doing real physical work in this formula, and it deserves attention before its own dedicated treatment as power factor. At θ = 0°, pure resistance, cos θ = 1 and all the apparent power converts to real, usable power. At θ = ±90°, pure inductance or pure capacitance, cos θ = 0 and average power is exactly zero, no net energy is delivered no matter how large the voltage and current are, because energy is only ever stored and returned, never consumed. Everywhere in between, only the resistive portion of the circuit actually dissipates energy; the reactive portion, examined next, still draws current and still stresses the wires and the source, but contributes nothing to this average.

There is a second, equivalent way to compute average power that applies directly to the resistor alone and offers a useful check: P = Irms² R. For the series RL circuit, Irms = 2.4 A and R = 30 Ω, so P = (2.4)² × 30 = 5.76 × 30 = 172.8 W, exactly matching the Vrms Irms cos θ calculation above. This agreement is not a coincidence: since the reactive element contributes nothing to average power, all of the real power in a series RL or RC circuit is dissipated in the resistor alone, so any formula correctly accounting for the resistor's dissipation must agree with the general Vrms Irms cos θ formula applied to the whole circuit.
